title: Choose Vera's family reader
question: Which reader world belongs in your kitchen? This is a local design choice only; nothing will publish.

options.label: Kitchen Timer Atlas
options.lineage: a mid-century kitchen timer and a household recipe index
options.thesis: A large recipe dial turns the family collection into a usable kitchen atlas.
options.viewport: A giant recipe dial fills the fold; the selected recipe opens as a calm reading tray beside it.
options.risk: The dial must remain a useful navigator, not a nostalgic prop.

options.label: Grid Recipe Specimen
options.thesis: The 110 recipes become a bold alphabetical instrument for finding what to cook.
options.viewport: Recipe initials form a monumental grid while the active recipe reads in a precise side column.
options.risk: The system can become cooler than the family stories it needs to carry.
options.case: Fuses cleanly: the recipe inventory gains exceptional scanability without pretending it is a generic recipe feed.

options.label: Family Recipe Issue
options.lineage: a mid-century magazine program with an abstract recurring mark
options.thesis: Each cookbook section becomes an issue to browse, read, and remember.
options.viewport: One full-bleed family-food image frames an opening recipe while a compact issue index anchors the reading path.
options.risk: It may feel like an archive publication before it feels useful at the stove.
options.case: Fuses cleanly: recipe families can become issues, but the cooking controls must stay more immediate than editorial decoration.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A straightforward cookbook library, executed with exceptional clarity.
canonCard.viewport: A familiar featured recipe with a searchable card grid below it.
canonCard.risk: It is dependable but could erase the collection's family-specific character.
